name: Mentawai
catalog_quote: Die Mehrzahl der Stammwörter ist ein- oder zweisilbig. Bei den zweisilbigen Wörtern ruht der Ton auf der vorletzten Silbe. Mit der Anhängung von Suffixen rückt auch der Ton zweisilbiger Wörter fort. ... Dreisilbige Wörter, die in nicht unbeträchtlicher Zahl vorhanden sind, haben den Ton in einigen wenigen Fällen auf der letzten, sonst auf der vorletzten oder drittvorletzten Silbe.

new_statements.quote: [p. 33] l en r als oorspronkelijke sluiters zijn bewaard gebleven doordat ze zijn klinkend gemaakt met een vocalischen naslag, die dezelfde is als de klinker der voorafgaande lettergreep. Daardoor wordt een nieuwe syllabe gevormd, die voor den klemtoon niet medetelt. Een oorspronkelijk bakoel „mand", met den klemtoon op ba, wordt dus bakoeloe, waarbij de klemtoon op ba blijft [...] [p. 84] In den 2den p. enk. wordt m gebruikt achter een woord dat op een korte open lettergreep eindigt, die geen klemtoon heeft; in alle andere gevallen staat -noe. [...] nini „voorvader", kebboe „oudere (broer, zuster)", oete „hoofd" (klemtoon resp. op ni, boe, te) vormen: [...] nininoe, kebboenoe, oetenoe.
new_statements.translation: [p. 33] l and r as original final consonants have been preserved by being made audible with a vocalic echo, which is the same as the vowel of the preceding syllable. Thereby a new syllable is formed, which does not count for the stress. An original bakoel 'basket', with the stress on ba, thus becomes bakoeloe, in which the stress stays on ba [...] [p. 84] In the 2nd person singular, m is used after a word ending in a short open syllable that has no stress; in all other cases -noe is used. [...] nini 'ancestor', kebboe 'elder (brother, sister)', oete 'head' (stress on ni, boe, te respectively) form: [...] nininoe, kebboenoe, oetenoe.
new_statements.citation: Adriani, N. (1928). Spraakkunstige schets van de taal der Mentawai-eilanden. Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 84(1): 1-117.
new_statements.locator: No section on stress; stress is mentioned in passing in §3 Tweeklanken pp. 10-12, §13 (final l/r with echo vowel) p. 33, and §37 Voornaamwoorden p. 84 (scan pages 29-31, 52, 103 of the PDF)
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences

Daardoor wordt een nieuwe syllabe gevormd, die voor den klemtoon niet medetelt. Een oorspronkelijk bakoel (Mal. id.) "mand", met den klemtoon op ba, wordt dus bakoeloe, waarbij de klemtoon op ba bl…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penultimate rule (StressTyp2) and adds detail: the echo-vowel final syllable from *l/*r is extrametrical (surface antepenult stress in bákoeloe etc.), and a handful of nouns are lexically final-stressed.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Adriani never states a general stress rule, but everything he says presupposes penultimate stress: Kruyt's examples on p. 10 are given with 'klemtoon op de voorlaatste' (leleoe 'forest') and every other example marked there (sikaola on kao, simoeine on moei, mapoeineng on poei, loina on loi, saoeloe on saoe, sikeili on kei, babaidjoe' on bai, kasooe on ka, lalaisoe on lai, kineneiget on nei) is penultimate once the diphthong counts as one syllable; ordinary disyllables like mata, mone, besi, toetoe have an unstressed final syllable (p. 84). Two refinements: (1) a final echo-vowel syllable created from historical final *l/*r 'does not count for the stress', so bakoeloe, póetere, pákoeroe, ábere, kókolo, kábili, sásala, tápolo, toekoeloe keep stress on the original penult (surface antepenult) (p. 33; p. 34 adds that in such languages speakers feel that syllable as the penult); (2) a few nouns carry final stress (nini, kebboe, oete), and stress placement is grammatically diagnostic: the 2sg possessive is -m after an unstressed short open final syllable, -noe elsewhere (p. 84). On p. 12 he adds that Mentawai, unlike Gorontalo, did not shift the stress when it made final consonants audible.
new_statements.exceptions: Final-stressed nouns nini 'ancestor', kebboe 'elder sibling', oete 'head' (p. 84); echo-vowel words with stress on the surface antepenult (bakoeloe, póetere, pákoeroe, ábere, kókolo, kábili, sásala, tápolo, p. 33). Diphthong-final words (laggai, alei, momoi) take -noe because a diphthong is not counted as an open syllable, not because of stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Adriani's sketch covers Mentawai in general, built on Max Morris's Die Mentawai-Sprache (1900), Dr. Kruyt's notes (the p. 10 stress examples are Kruyt's) and corrections from missionary O. Werkman of North Pagai; he notes northern (Siberut) versus southern (Sipora/Pagai) dialect differences elsewhere but none of the stress remarks is tied to a particular dialect.

audit.recode_to: fixed penult, NON-strict (not in the strict set; lexical oxytones e.g. utä 'head', ubä 'tobacco', udät 'sit' and a proparoxytone class bákala/tükulu per Morris 1900 §2 pp.4-6), with a caution flag: later descriptions conflict — Lenggang et al. 1978 p.14-15: level stress in disyllables, penult in 3+ syllables, non-phonemic; Arifin, Malano & Kasim 1992 p.101-102: final stress 'like Indonesian', non-distinctive. If the catalog has a 'weak/non-contrastive word stress, penult~final variably reported' category, that is the honest home.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is present verbatim at Morris 1900 §2 p.4 in the djvu text we hold (lines 520-547). (2) But the classification 'fixed-strict' penult (penultimate stress) over-reads its own source: on the same pages Morris gives a closed list of ~19 disyllabic oxytones and ~60 trisyllabic proparoxytones ('haben den ursprünglichen Accent bewahrt'), plus a residual trisyllabic oxytone (gorosot) — so 'strict' is not supported even by Morris. (3) The deciding source is a 1900 sketch from a short field trip whose author disclaims attention to fine pronunciation; Glottolog lists five later descriptive works including a 160-pp phonology. (4) I downloaded the two open ones from the Internet Archive copies of the Kemdikbud repository: Lenggang et al. 1978 (pp.14-15) says disyllables carry equal stress on both syllables and 3+-syllable words generally penultimate primary stress, non-phonemic; Arifin

sources.quote: 'Tekanan ternyata tidak membedakan arti (non-phonemic). ... pada umumnya, imbuhan tidak mendapat tekanan utama. Kata-kata yang terdiri dari dua suku kata, kedua suku kata itu, umumnya, mendapat tekanan yang sama [e.g. iba 'ikan', sara 'satu'] ... Kata-kata yang terdiri dari tiga atau lebih suku kata, tekanan utama (primary stress), pada umumnya, jatuh pada suku kedua dari akhir (penultimate)' [e.g. maígi, sirimanúa, sinanálep]. [Stress non-phonemic; affixes generally unstressed; disyllables: both syllables equally stressed; 3+ syllables: primary stress generally penultimate.]
sources.locator: §2.7 'Ciri Prosodi', a. Tekanan Kata, printed pp. 14-15 (PDF pp. 25-26); text layer lines 842-880
sources.note: Structural sketch with a prosody section (§2.7): penult in 3+-syllable words but level stress in disyllables, non-phonemic, affixes unstressed — refines/weakens 'fixed-strict'.

sources.quote: 'Dalam bahasa Mentawai tekanan kata terdengar seperti yang dijumpai dalam bahasa Indonesia. Bila sebuah kata terdiri dari dua suku kata, tekanan jatuh pada suku akhir. Selanjutnya, bila sebuah kata terdiri dari tiga suku kata, maka suku akhir mendapat tekanan keras (tekanan primer) dan suku kedua mendapat tekanan lemah (tekanan sekunder). Namun ... kehadiran tekanan yang berbeda dalam bahasa Mentawai tidak menimbulkan makna yang berbeda.'
